name: Coeruleum
lede: Coeruleum is the older spelling of cerulean, the cobalt-tin blue that painters took up in the 1860s, though its story starts with an obscure German recipe from 1789.

sections.title: Cerulean and ceruleum
sections.body:
Paterson sends *coeruleum* to *cerulean blue*, which he describes as a bright, light greenish-blue pigment from chromium, cobalt and tin oxides and discovered in 1860 by George Rowney and Son [1]. The Pigment Compendium cautions that the literature mixes the spellings *cerulean* and *ceruleum*, with *coelin* and *caeruleum* as relatives [2]. Church in 1901 used *cœruleum* as his main heading, and by 1935 Doerner made cerulean the main term and coeruleum a synonym [2].

The root is Latin *caeruleus*, which meant dark blue or dark green, and the English word is recorded as early as the seventeenth century [2]. The French trade used *bleu cœruleum* and *bleu céleste*, the celestial blue [2].

sections.title: Who made it first
sections.body:
The books disagree on the date. Paterson gives 1860 and Rowney [1]. Coffignier put it about 1850, but Carlyle's research, reported in the Compendium, shows it unlikely before 1862 or 1863 [2]. Just before that, the London firm Roberson was buying a *Blue 58 (Cerulium)* from the German firm of Frauenknecht and Stotz [2]. That fits Salter's note of 1869 that a cobalt-tin blue called coelin had lately been imported from Germany [2].

There were precursors. Höpfner described a cobalt-tin blue in 1789, and Schreger listed it as a beautiful painter's color in 1805 [2]. It then seems to have been largely forgotten until the 1850s and 1860s [2].

The recipe also varied. Ure's mid-century text gives stannate of cobalt with stannic acid and sulphate of lime, while Paterson names chromium instead of lime [2][1]. One analysis found chromium cobalt aluminium oxide in some acrylics sold as cerulean, though that appears rare [2].

sections.title: Not the Roman caeruleum
sections.body: The Compendium files the Latin *caeruleum* with Egyptian blue, a copper-calcium silicate, and cites Pliny and Vitruvius for it [2]. Paterson, too, lists coeruleum among the "colores floridi", the costly ancient pigments, with cinnabar and indigo [1]. So the old name belonged to another blue, and the nineteenth-century paint inherited the word rather than the recipe [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: This swatch comes from Maerz and Paul in 1930 [3]. It is a medium, fairly saturated blue, called vivid blue by the ISCC-NBS system and 7.3 CIEDE2000 units from that region [3]. Paterson's cerulean is a light greenish blue, so the chart color is deeper and bluer than his description [1][3]. Related names are [[cerulean-blue]], [[cobalt-blue]] and [[celestial-blue]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color is uncommon in paint. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 27 works [4]. Seven in ten of those appearances are mid-tones [4]. The earliest dated painting in the wider match is Fra Angelico's of 1426, which long predates the pigment, so it shows how much a screen color proves [4]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, not pigment tests [4].

origin.first_recorded: English cerulean in the 17th century; the pigment 1860s

disambiguation.gloss: the general sky-blue word, not the pigment

questions.q: Why do dates for cerulean blue vary between books?
choices: Its origin is unclear and earlier cobalt-tin blues existed
It was only invented in the 1900s
questions.answer: Its origin is unclear and earlier cobalt-tin blues existed

questions.q: True or false: the Roman caeruleum was the same pigment as nineteenth-century cerulean.

openers: A cobalt-tin blue was described in 1789 and then forgotten for decades before cerulean took off.
Cerulean's first maker is disputed: Rowney 1860, or Germans selling to London around 1862.
